title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about creativity at university: what it really means and why it matters in every subject. By the end you will be able to explain that creativity is a skill you can build, tell divergent thinking apart from convergent thinking, and recognise the barriers that get in the way.

Creativity is not only for artists or for people who feel naturally inventive. Generating ideas, making unexpected connections and approaching a problem from several angles are things every student does, and every student can get better at. Building this now changes how you tackle essays, projects and problems across your degree.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain that creativity is a developable academic skill, not an innate gift
distinguish divergent thinking from convergent thinking
recognise common barriers to creativity and how to work past them.

title: In real academic practice
body: Creativity is a habit academic work rewards far more than students expect. Every essay that asks for an argument of your own, every project that needs a fresh angle, every problem without a set answer draws on the same skill. Build it now and it carries into every module of your degree, and into the problem-solving that professional work later asks of you.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, creativity as a skill: what the word really means at university. Second, divergent and convergent thinking: the two modes behind creative work. Third, getting past the barriers: what blocks creativity and how to move through it. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: Many students believe creativity is a gift: you either have it or you do not, and it belongs to artists rather than to their subject. This lesson sets that idea aside. Creativity is a skill that can be learned and strengthened, and it matters in every discipline. We look at what it actually is, so it stops being a mystery and starts being something you can build.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are early in your studies, and creativity may be new as something to work on deliberately. At this stage you are not expected to produce strikingly original work. The aim is to recognise creative thinking when you see it and to understand what it is, the foundation you will build on as you progress.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain that creativity is a developable skill, not a gift some people are simply born with
recognise creativity at work in a worked example of a student's approach
identify what creativity looks like in an academic task in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Creativity is not a fixed trait that some people have and others lack. It is a skill: a way of thinking that can be practised and improved, like any other. To be creative is to generate new ideas, make connections that others miss, and look at a problem from more than one angle.

This matters because university rewards ideas of your own, not only the recall of other people's. Creativity is not the opposite of being rigorous, either. It generates the possibilities, and critical thinking then weighs them. This lesson is about what creativity is; the lessons that follow are about how it works and what gets in its way.

You can now explain what creativity is and recognise it in how a student approaches a task. The next lessons turn this into practice: the two modes of thinking behind creative work, and the barriers that get in the way.

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you saw that creativity is a skill you can build. This lesson is about how creative thinking actually works. It has two modes, and good creative work uses both: one mode opens things up and generates possibilities, the other narrows down and chooses. Knowing which mode you are in, and when to switch, is what turns raw ideas into finished work.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to master a full creative method yet. The aim here is to notice the difference between thinking that generates ideas and thinking that judges them, and to see why doing both at the same time tends to stop either from working well.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: tell divergent thinking apart from convergent thinking
give an example of generating ideas before judging them
choose the right mode of thinking for a stage of an academic task in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Creative thinking moves between two modes. Divergent thinking opens a problem up: you generate many possibilities, follow unlikely ideas, and hold back from judging. Convergent thinking closes it down: you compare the options, weigh them, and choose the strongest. Neither mode is the whole of creativity; the skill is using each at the right time.

The common mistake is to run both at once, judging each idea the moment it arrives. That tends to shut down the flow of possibilities before any have had a chance. Generating first and judging second is why brainstorming separates the two. This is also where creativity and critical thinking meet: creativity generates the ideas, and critical thinking evaluates them.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about how you usually start a piece of work. Do you generate several ideas first, or judge each one as it arrives? What might change if you kept the two apart?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Creative thinking uses two modes: divergent thinking generates possibilities, and convergent thinking narrows them to the strongest. You can now tell the two apart, see why generating should come before judging, and choose the mode that fits the stage you are at. The next lesson looks at the barriers that stop this working, and how to move past them.

title: Orientation
body: You have seen that creativity is a skill, and that it works through generating ideas and then choosing among them. So why does it so often feel blocked? This lesson looks at the barriers that get in the way. Most are not about ability at all; they are habits of mind, and once you can name them you can begin to work past them.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to overcome every barrier at once. The aim is to recognise the common ones when they show up in your own work, and to know one practical move that loosens each, so a blank page feels less like a verdict on whether you are creative.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise common barriers to creativity, such as fear of failure and perfectionism
tell a barrier to creativity apart from a habit that helps it
choose a way past a barrier when starting a creative task in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
The barriers to creativity are mostly habits of mind rather than limits on talent. Fear of failure makes you stay with the safe, obvious idea rather than risk a weak one. Perfectionism makes you judge every idea before it is finished, so nothing rough survives long enough to grow. The pressure to be right first time rushes you past the generating stage altogether.

Working past them starts with a single shift: give yourself permission to produce rough or 'bad' ideas on purpose. A bad idea is often a step towards a good one, and separating generating from judging keeps the inner critic quiet while possibilities build. The barrier is real, but it is not fixed, and small changes in how you work loosen it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Which of the barriers in this lesson do you recognise most in your own work? What is one small thing you could try next time to loosen it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: The barriers to creativity, such as fear of failure, perfectionism and the pressure to be right first time, are habits of mind rather than limits on talent. You can now recognise them, tell a barrier apart from a habit that helps, and choose a move that loosens one. With the skill, the two modes and the barriers in view, you are ready to build your creativity on purpose.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Creativity is no longer a vague gift that belongs to other people: it is a skill you can describe and begin to build. You can explain that creativity is developable and matters in every subject. You can tell divergent thinking, which generates ideas, apart from convergent thinking, which chooses among them. And you can name the barriers, such as fear of failure and perfectionism, and a move that loosens each. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, creativity is something you practise in every module. Each time you generate options before choosing, each unexpected connection you follow, each rough idea you let live long enough to grow, is the skill at work. It is also what professional life rewards: the ability to find fresh angles and turn ideas into action travels well beyond your degree.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced creativity courses take the skill into creative methods for real study tasks, and then into innovation, enterprise and professional practice. Going wider: the same habits underpin Criticality, Reflective Practice and Researching, where you put creative thinking to work alongside other skills.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Creativity: a key term
instruction: Select the card to reveal more about this term.
definition: The skill of generating new ideas, making unexpected connections, and seeing a problem from more than one angle.
extendedDefinition: At university, creativity is a developable skill that matters in every subject, not an artistic gift reserved for a few. It generates the possibilities, which critical thinking then weighs.
example: A student lists several possible essay questions before choosing, then connects two of them into an angle of their own.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Consider two students given the same open-ended assignment: find an interesting question about the topic and explore it.

{{learner-a}} picks the first question that comes to mind, the one the lecturer already used as an example, and writes it up. The task is done, safely. But {{learner-a}} settled on a single obvious idea without looking for others, treating creativity as something the assignment did not really need. This is the fixed view of creativity: leave it to people who have it.

{{learner-b}} jots down several possible questions first, including a few that seem unlikely, then looks for an angle that connects two of them in a way the reading had not. The question that results is the student's own. This is creativity as a skill: generate options, make a connection, then choose.

Both students completed the task. Only {{learner-b}} treated creativity as something to practise, turning a safe answer into an idea of their own.

title: Creative habits
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These habits turn creativity from a mystery into something you do. Try them on your next open task.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I written down several ideas before choosing one?
Have I let myself note a rough or unlikely idea without dismissing it?
Have I looked for a connection between two ideas that seem unrelated?
Have I asked how the problem looks from a different angle?
Have I separated generating ideas from judging them, rather than doing both at once?
Have I treated a first attempt as a draft to improve, not a verdict on my ability?

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: From many ideas to the right one
body: The two modes of creative thinking, step by step. Reveal each stage to see how divergent thinking hands over to convergent thinking.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Open the problem up
_items.body: Start by generating as many ideas as you can, including unlikely ones. Hold back from judging; here the goal is range and quantity, not quality yet.

_items.title: Follow unexpected connections
_items.body: Look across your ideas for links between ones that seem unrelated. A connection between two rough ideas is often where something original begins.

_items.title: Narrow down and choose
_items.body: Now switch modes. Compare the options, weigh them against what the task needs, and choose the strongest. This is convergent thinking.

_items.title: Refine the choice
_items.body: Develop the idea you chose, test it, and improve it. If it does not hold up, you still have the other ideas to return to.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students sit down to plan the same essay, with twenty minutes before a seminar.

{{learner-a}} picks an argument straight away and starts writing it up, judging each sentence as it comes. Twenty minutes later there is half a paragraph, each line reworked twice. {{learner-a}} ran both modes at once, generating and judging in the same breath, so very little was generated and even less survived.

{{learner-b}} spends the first ten minutes listing every angle on the question, good and bad, without stopping to judge. Then, in the second ten, {{learner-b}} reads the list, crosses out the weak ones, and picks the two that connect into an argument. Generating first and choosing second produced more to work with, and a stronger choice.

Both had the same twenty minutes. Only {{learner-b}} kept the two modes apart, which is what let the ideas flow and then settle.

title: Working in the two modes
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These moves keep divergent and convergent thinking apart. Try them on your next piece of work.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I generated several ideas before judging any of them?
When generating, did I let unlikely ideas onto the list?
Did I look for connections between ideas that seemed unrelated?
When choosing, did I weigh the options against what the task needs?
Did I notice which mode I was in, generating or choosing?
Did I avoid polishing one idea before I had a few to compare?

title: Formative check: divergent versus convergent
displayTitle: Which of these describes divergent thinking rather than convergent thinking?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option describes divergent thinking rather than convergent thinking?

_items.text: Generating many possible ideas, including unlikely ones, without judging yet.
_items.feedback: Yes. Opening up and generating possibilities is divergent thinking.

_items.text: Comparing the options and choosing the strongest one.
_items.feedback: That is convergent thinking, which narrows down.

_items.text: Polishing a single idea until it is finished.
_items.feedback: Polishing one idea is neither generating nor really choosing among options.

_items.text: Checking your final answer against the marking criteria.
_items.feedback: That is a late, convergent step, not generating ideas.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Divergent thinking opens the problem up by generating many possibilities.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option is about generating ideas rather than narrowing them?
_incorrect.final: Divergent thinking generates many possibilities without judging yet. Comparing, choosing and checking are all convergent, narrowing moves.

title: Formative check: keeping the modes apart
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student do that let the ideas flow?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second student do that let the ideas flow?

_items.text: Generated a list of angles first, without judging, then chose afterwards.
_items.feedback: Yes. Keeping generating and judging apart is what let the ideas flow.

_items.text: Started writing the argument straight away and judged each line.
_items.feedback: That is what the first student did, and it generated very little.

_items.text: Spent the whole time polishing one sentence.
_items.feedback: Polishing one sentence is the opposite of generating options.

_items.text: Waited for a single good idea to arrive.
_items.feedback: The student generated many ideas rather than waiting for one.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student generated first and judged second, keeping the two modes apart.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that separated generating from judging.
_incorrect.final: The ideas flowed because the second student generated a list first and judged afterwards. Writing straight away, polishing one line, or waiting for one idea all collapse the two modes together.

title: Formative check: choosing the mode
displayTitle: You are at the start of an open task in {{context}} and need ideas. Which mode of thinking fits this stage?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which mode of thinking fits the idea-generating stage of a task?

_items.text: Divergent thinking: generate several possibilities before judging any.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, the start of an open task calls for generating possibilities.

_items.text: Convergent thinking: pick the first workable idea and commit.
_items.feedback: Committing early skips the generating this stage needs.

_items.text: Judging each idea the moment it occurs to you.
_items.feedback: Judging too early shuts down the flow of ideas.

_items.text: Waiting until the best idea arrives on its own.
_items.feedback: Ideas are generated deliberately here, not waited for.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The start of an open task in {{context}} calls for divergent thinking: generate first, judge later.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which mode generates possibilities rather than narrowing them?
_incorrect.final: At the start of an open task in {{context}} you need divergent thinking, generating possibilities first. Committing early, judging at once, or waiting all cut the generating short.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The barriers, and how to loosen each
body: Four common barriers to creativity. Read each card to see what it is and one move that loosens it.
instruction: Read through the cards below.
ariaRegion: Information cards about barriers to creativity.

_items.title: Fear of failure
_items.subtitle: The safe choice
_items.text: You stay with the obvious idea rather than risk a weak one. The move that loosens it: treat early ideas as low-stakes attempts, not a test of your ability.

_items.title: Perfectionism
_items.subtitle: Judging too early
_items.text: You polish or reject each idea before it is finished, so nothing rough survives. The move that loosens it: separate generating from judging, and let rough ideas exist first.

_items.title: Right first time
_items.subtitle: Rushing the start
_items.text: You jump straight to the answer, past the stage where ideas are generated. The move that loosens it: give the generating stage its own time before you choose.

_items.title: The inner critic
_items.subtitle: The blocking voice
_items.text: A running commentary that dismisses ideas as they arrive. The move that loosens it: allow 'bad' ideas on purpose, since a bad idea is often a step towards a good one.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students face the same open brief: propose your own project on the module theme.

{{learner-a}} stares at the blank page, waiting for a good idea to arrive fully formed. Every idea that comes is dismissed as too obvious or too risky before it is even written down. An hour later the page is still empty, and {{learner-a}} concludes they are just not a creative person. The barrier was not a lack of ideas; it was judging each one before it had a chance.

{{learner-b}} sets a timer and writes down ten ideas, allowing them to be rough or odd, with no judging until the timer stops. Several are weak. But two can be combined, and one of the odd ones turns out to be the most promising. The page filled because the inner critic was kept waiting.

Both students had the same brief and the same doubts. Only {{learner-b}} gave rough ideas room to appear before judging them.

title: Loosening a barrier
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These moves loosen the common barriers. Try them next time a creative task feels blocked.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I named the barrier that is actually stopping me?
Did I let myself write a rough or 'bad' idea on purpose?
Did I give the generating stage its own time before choosing?
Did I keep judging separate from generating?
Have I treated a first attempt as a draft, not a verdict on my ability?
Did I follow an odd idea far enough to see where it led?

ariaQuestion: Which statement best describes creativity at university?

_items.text: A skill you can practise and build, useful in any subject.
_items.feedback: Yes. Creativity is a developable skill across the disciplines.

_items.text: A gift that some students are born with and others are not.
_items.feedback: That is the fixed view the course sets aside.

_items.text: A style that belongs to the arts and to creative writing.
_items.feedback: Creativity matters in every subject.

_items.text: A talent that only matters on design or art courses.
_items.feedback: Ideas and connections matter in all disciplines.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Creativity is a skill you can build, in any subject.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about whether creativity is fixed or developable.

body: Which of these best shows creativity treated as a skill rather than a fixed gift?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which best shows creativity treated as a skill?

_items.text: Generating several ideas and connecting two into an angle of your own.
_items.feedback: Yes. Generating and connecting is creativity as a practised skill.

_items.text: Waiting until you feel naturally inspired before starting.
_items.feedback: Waiting for inspiration is the fixed view.

_items.text: Choosing the first, most obvious idea to be safe.
_items.feedback: The safe, single idea skips the generating creativity needs.

_items.text: Leaving the ideas to the people who are naturally creative.
_items.feedback: That treats creativity as a gift rather than a skill.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Generating ideas and connecting them is creativity as a skill.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that generates and connects ideas.

body: A student generates many possible ideas without judging them yet. This is an example of...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Generating many ideas without judging yet is an example of...

_items.text: divergent thinking.
_items.feedback: Yes. Opening up and generating possibilities is divergent thinking.

_items.text: convergent thinking.
_items.feedback: Convergent thinking narrows down and chooses.

_items.text: perfectionism.
_items.feedback: Perfectionism judges ideas too early; here no judging is happening.

_items.text: proofreading.
_items.feedback: Proofreading is a late check, not idea generation.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Generating possibilities without judging is divergent thinking.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which mode opens a problem up rather than narrowing it?

body: Why does this course recommend generating ideas before judging them?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why generate ideas before judging them?

_items.text: Judging each idea as it arrives tends to shut down the flow of possibilities.
_items.feedback: Yes. Judging too early stops ideas before they can build.

_items.text: Judging ideas early always produces the best single answer.
_items.feedback: Judging too early tends to cut the range of ideas short.

_items.text: Ideas should never be judged at all in academic work.
_items.feedback: They are judged, but at the convergent stage, after generating.

_items.text: Generating and judging are really the same activity.
_items.feedback: They are two different modes, which is why keeping them apart helps.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Judging too early shuts down the flow, so generating comes first.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what happens when you judge each idea at once.

body: Which of these is a barrier to creativity rather than a help?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option is a barrier to creativity rather than a help?

_items.text: Perfectionism that rejects every idea before it is finished.
_items.feedback: Yes. Judging ideas too harshly, too early, is a barrier.

_items.text: Writing down rough ideas to develop later.
_items.feedback: That is a helpful habit, not a barrier.

_items.text: Giving the generating stage its own time.
_items.feedback: That helps creativity rather than blocking it.

_items.text: Following an odd idea to see where it leads.
_items.feedback: That is a creative move, not a barrier.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Perfectionism that rejects ideas too early is a barrier.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the habit that blocks ideas rather than helping them.

body: What is the single move this course recommends for getting past a creative block?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What single move gets past a creative block?

_items.text: Give yourself permission to produce rough or 'bad' ideas on purpose.
_items.feedback: Yes. Allowing rough ideas keeps the inner critic waiting and gets you moving.

_items.text: Wait until a polished, finished idea arrives.
_items.feedback: Waiting for a finished idea is what leaves the page blank.

_items.text: Choose the safest, most obvious idea every time.
_items.feedback: Playing safe is the barrier, not the way past it.

_items.text: Decide your subject has no room for your own ideas.
_items.feedback: That belief is itself a barrier to creativity.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Allowing rough ideas on purpose is the move that loosens a block.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which move lets rough ideas appear rather than blocking them?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: creativity as a skill, the two modes of thinking, and the barriers that get in the way. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to run a polished creative method. The aim is to see creativity as one working practice rather than three separate ideas, so it carries on into the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise how creativity as a skill, the two modes of thinking and getting past the barriers connect as one practice
show the three working together in a worked example of a student's ongoing study
plan one way to keep using the three together in your {{context}} study beyond this course

title: Concept: definition
body: A working creative practice is these three ideas used together, on purpose. You treat creativity as a skill, you move between generating ideas and choosing among them, and you keep the barriers loose by letting rough ideas exist. It is not three separate lessons but one habit you bring to any open task.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, a working creative practice is something you bring to any open task, in any subject. You treat the task as a chance to practise, give yourself room to generate rough ideas, then choose and refine the strongest. The more often you run it, the more natural each part becomes.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of one open task coming up in your studies, such as an essay, a project or a problem with no set answer. How will you run the whole practice on it: treat it as a skill, generate before judging, and keep rough ideas alive?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Creativity is most useful when it becomes a working practice. You treat it as a skill, move between generating and choosing, and keep the barriers loose, again and again. It is the habit, not any single idea, that improves how you study.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: A working creative practice is a continuing habit, not a one-off. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Treat as practice
_items.body: Treat the task as a chance to practise creativity, not a test of a gift you have or lack.

_items.title: Open up
_items.body: Open the problem up - generate several ideas, including rough ones, without judging them yet.

_items.title: Narrow down
_items.body: Narrow down - compare your ideas and choose the strongest for what the task needs.

_items.title: Refine and carry
_items.body: Refine your choice, then carry the same practice into your next task. The cycle keeps turning.

_diagram.title: Creative practice as a continuing habit

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students face the same open brief. One waits for a single good idea, judges it at once, and treats creativity as a gift they may not have. The other treats it as a practice: they list rough ideas, keep the best alive, then choose and refine. Over the term, the second student's work grows stronger, because creativity became a habit rather than a one-off.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to keep creativity working
body: Use these to keep the whole practice going, rather than leaning on only one part of it.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I treat this task as creativity I can practise, not a gift I either have or lack?
Did I generate several ideas before choosing any of them?
Did I let rough or unlikely ideas onto the list first?
Did I keep generating and judging apart, rather than doing both at once?
Did I carry the practice into my next task, not just this one?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat creativity as one working practice rather than three separate ideas?
body: Why is it more useful to treat creativity as one working practice rather than three separate ideas?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat creativity as one working practice rather than three separate ideas?

_items.text: Because the three parts feed each other: you treat it as a skill, generate then choose, and keep the barriers loose, all on the same task.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three ideas are parts of one habit, used together on a single task.

_items.text: Because learning one of the three ideas on its own fixes how you work for good.
_items.feedback: Not quite. Each idea is only part of the practice; they work best together.

_items.text: Because a single practice means you never have to judge your ideas.
_items.feedback: Judging is part of the practice. Convergent thinking is how you choose the strongest idea.

_items.text: Because treating creativity as one practice takes less thought than using the three ideas.
_items.feedback: The point is not less thought. It is that the three parts support each other.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The skill, the two modes and the barriers are parts of one working practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how the three ideas support each other on the same task.

displayTitle: A student faces an open essay question. They treat it as a chance to practise, list several rough ideas without judging, then choose and refine the strongest. What does this show?
body: A student faces an open essay question. They treat it as a chance to practise, list several rough ideas without judging, then choose and refine the strongest. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student faces an open essay question. They treat it as a chance to practise, list several rough ideas without judging, then choose and refine the strongest. What does this show?

_items.text: That creativity is working as one practice: the skill, the two modes and loosening the barriers all turn up on the same task.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three ideas are at work together, which is what the practice looks like.

_items.text: That the student is naturally gifted and did not need to practise.
_items.feedback: The student practised on purpose. That is the skill at work, not a gift.

_items.text: That generating ideas is the only part of creativity that matters.
_items.feedback: Generating is one part. The student also chose and refined, which is convergent thinking.

_items.text: That judging ideas early is the best way to start an essay.
_items.feedback: The student held judging back at first. That is what let the rough ideas appear.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three ideas are working together as one practice on a single task.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how the student used all three ideas on the same task.

displayTitle: You want to use creativity as a working practice to study {{context}} better this term. Which plan keeps all three parts in play?
body: You want to use creativity as a working practice to study {{context}} better this term. Which plan keeps all three parts in play?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use creativity as a working practice to study your subject better this term. Which plan keeps all three parts in play?

_items.text: On each open task, treat it as a skill, generate ideas before judging, keep rough ideas alive, then choose and refine.
_items.feedback: Yes. That keeps the skill, the two modes and the loosened barriers all working together.

_items.text: Wait for good ideas to arrive, and only start when one feels right.
_items.feedback: That leaves out generating rough ideas, and it treats creativity as a gift you wait for.

_items.text: Generate lots of ideas, but never stop to choose between them.
_items.feedback: Generating alone is not enough. Convergent thinking is how you choose the strongest idea.

_items.text: Judge each idea the moment it arrives, so you do not waste time.
_items.feedback: Judging too early shuts down the ideas before they can grow. Keep generating and judging apart.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Using all three parts on each task keeps creativity working as a practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan keeps the skill, the two modes and the barriers all in play.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Which statement best describes creativity as a working practice?
body: Which statement best describes creativity as a working practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement best describes creativity as a working practice?

_items.text: It is the skill, the two modes of thinking, and getting past the barriers used together on a task.
_items.feedback: Yes. The practice brings all three ideas together.

_items.text: It is choosing the single best idea as quickly as possible.
_items.feedback: That is only convergent thinking, one part of the practice.

_items.text: It is a gift that lets some people skip the hard parts.
_items.feedback: Creativity is a skill you practise, not a gift.

_items.text: It is generating as many ideas as possible and stopping there.
_items.feedback: Generating is one part. You also choose and refine.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student keeps a rough idea alive, builds on it, then chooses and refines it across a term of projects. Which best describes what they are doing?
body: A student keeps a rough idea alive, builds on it, then chooses and refines it across a term of projects. Which best describes what they are doing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student keeps a rough idea alive, builds on it, then chooses and refines it across a term of projects. Which best describes what they are doing?

_items.text: Using creativity as a continuing working practice across their studies.
_items.feedback: Yes. The practice is repeated across tasks, not used once.

_items.text: Relying on a natural gift rather than a skill.
_items.feedback: Keeping and building ideas on purpose is the skill at work.

_items.text: Judging every idea the moment it arrives.
_items.feedback: They kept a rough idea alive, which is the opposite of judging too early.

_items.text: Skipping the choosing stage of creative work.
_items.feedback: They chose and refined, so convergent thinking was part of it.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
